highlights.titleZh: Argonne-Led CoLA Approach Makes LLM Pre-Training More Efficient
highlights.content: ### TCI Media: Home of the Wire Publications ![Header Logo 1](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/ai-600-300x73-1.webp) ![Header Logo 2](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/bigdatawire-logo.webp) ![Header Logo 3](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/qc-600-300x69-1.webp) ![Logo](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/hpc-logo-300x60-1.jpg) ## Off the Wire Press Releases ### August 12, 2026 ### August 11, 2026 ### August 10, 2026 ### August 7, 2026 ## Argonne-Led CoLA Approach Makes LLM Pre-Training More Efficient Aug. 12, 2026 — CoLA might sound like a soft drink, but in computing it’s a new approach for pre-training large language models (LLMs). Developed by researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy’s [Argonne National Laboratory](https://www.anl.gov/), the University of California, Santa Barbara and the University at Albany, SUNY, Compute-Efficient Pre-Training of LLMs via Low-Rank Activation (CoLA) aims to make model training faster, cheaper and more efficient. ![](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/cola_web_1-300x169.jpg) By reducing the number of activation functions, CoLA-M greatly improves the memory saving, outperforming even the “vanilla” implementation of gradient checkpointing (GCP). **Breaking Free from an Unsustainable Trend** LLMs keep becoming bigger, needing more GPUs to provide the necessary power for pre-training over longer periods of time. Researchers have tried to address this trend by simplifying models using ​“low-rank” techniques, but many of these approaches increase computing costs, use too much memory or reduce model quality. CoLA takes a different path. Instead of relying on very large and complex layers commonly used in LLMs, CoLA uses *bottleneck-structured auto-encoders,* comprising low-weight matrices and a nonlinear activation in the middle. Normally, the word *bottleneck* sounds like a bad thing — a place where everything slows down. In CoLA, however, the bottleneck structure is intentional and helpful. “The key insight is that many of the model activations in pre-trained LLMs are redundant,” said Ziyue Liu, a PhD candidate at UC Santa Barbara and a visiting student at Argonne’s Mathematics and Computer Science (MCS) division. ​“By selecting the rank to be significantly smaller than the input/output dimensions, we create a narrow ​‘bottleneck’ that forces the data into a smaller space. Working in this space, CoLA avoids carrying out inefficient, redundant operations and focuses only on what matters most.” When tested with popular LLaMA models, CoLA used fewer parameters and cut computations by about half — without hurting performance during training. **Providing a New Variant** Just as cola soft drinks come in different flavors, CoLA provides a variant, CoLA-M, specifically designed to save memory. “Again, we take advantage of the bottleneck structure,” said Ruijie Zhang, a predoctoral appointee in Argonne’s MCS division and a co-author of the CoLA study. ​“Our CoLA-M implementation stores only the low-rank activations and recomputes the rest when needed, instead of keeping everything in memory. This approach significantly reduces memory demands without slowing down training.” Compared with other memory-saving techniques — which often add extra computation or reduce accuracy — CoLA-M performs exceptionally well. It cuts overall memory use by about two-thirds, surpassing even the most effective implementation (i.e., ​“vanilla” gradient checkpointing, GCP, which saves only one intermediate result from each transformer layer) while being 5x cheaper in precomputation and 3x cheaper in total computation. **Faster Training, Too** Efficiency isn’t just about computation and memory — it’s also about speed. Many existing low-rank methods slow training because they add extra steps. In contrast, both CoLA and CoLA-M deliver higher training throughput...

[Yash @ Explainx](https://substack.com/@goyashy) This week in AI, the spotlight is on **robot learning, local AI inference, and the evolving creator economy**. From Dyna Robotics using massive volumes of human video to teach robots physical skills, to MiniMax H3 bringing advanced AI inference closer to consumer hardware, and YouTube reshaping creator monetization for 2027, the industry is moving toward AI that can learn from real-world data, run more locally, and create new economic opportunities. * **Dyna-2 is training robots on 1 million+ hours of human video**, exploring how large-scale human activity data can help robots understand and perform physical tasks. The research points toward a future where robots can learn more efficiently without relying solely on robot-specific training data. * **MiniMax H3 is coming to Mac through an open-source inference engine**, giving developers a way to experiment with the model locally rather than depending entirely on cloud infrastructure. The project reflects growing interest in running capable AI models directly on consumer hardware. * **YouTube is changing its Partner Program for 2027**, introducing new monetization opportunities across Premium Lite, Shorts, shopping, and brand partnerships. The updates signal a broader push to give creators more ways to earn beyond traditional advertising. Together, these developments highlight a broader shift in AI: models are moving closer to the physical world, becoming easier to run locally, and creating new opportunities for the people building and distributing digital content. --- ### Dyna-2 Trains Robots on 1 Million+ Hours of Human Video Dyna Robotics has introduced Dyna-2, a world-action-reasoning model pretrained on more than 1 million hours of egocentric human video. The research explores whether increasing the amount of human video data can improve a model’s ability to understand actions and transfer that knowledge across different physical embodiments, including robots. Dyna says its experiments demonstrate scaling behavior on both human and robot evaluations, suggesting that large-scale human video could become an important source of training data for robots. The work points toward a future where robots can learn physical skills from the vast amount of video humans already generate, potentially reducing the need for collecting massive amounts of robot-specific training data. ## MiniMax H3 Gets a Lightweight Mac Inference Engine A new open-source project on GitHub, h3.c, brings a MiniMax H3 inference engine to Mac computers. The project focuses on making the model easier to run locally, giving developers a way to experiment with H3 without relying entirely on cloud-based inference. The repository is written in C and released under the MIT license, making it accessible for developers who want to inspect, modify, or integrate the implementation into their own projects. The project has also quickly attracted attention from the open-source community, showing growing interest in running advanced generative AI models directly on consumer hardware. ## YouTube Changes Its Partner Program for 2027 YouTube is making its first major changes to the YouTube Partner Program since 2018, with a stronger focus on rewarding active creators and expanding ways to earn. The platform says the program now includes more than 3 million creators, and upcoming changes will introduce new monetization opportunities while adjusting some existing requirements. Cerebras' super-fast inference solution should help it gain a foothold in the huge market. AMD is aggressively tackling inference from multiple angles. Inference has become the fastest-growing part of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure market, and Bloomberg Intelligence projects it will double the size of the AI training market by 2032, reaching $1.3 trillion. With so much at stake, both leading chipmakers and upstarts are jockeying to grab a slice of this huge, fast-growing market. **Nvidia**(NASDAQ: NVDA), **Cerebras**(NASDAQ: CBRS), and **Advanced Micro Devices**(NASDAQ: AMD) are all tackling this market in different ways. Let's see how these [AI stocks](https://www.fool.com/investing/stock-market/market-sectors/information-technology/ai-stocks/?utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=55fb489e-526f-4d57-8e99-2aab968f43fd) stack up and why they could all be winners, given the size and growth of the inference market. ***Missed Nvidia in 2009? This collaboration will utilise Nvidia's latest systems to provide inference for open-source AI models, addressing rising demand for computing capacity in cloud environments. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Aug 12, 2026 at 08:50 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * IBM and Together AI signed a $240 million multi-year agreement for an AI cluster. * The cluster will be built on IBM Cloud using Nvidia's HGX B300 systems and Blackwell processors. * It aims to provide inference capabilities for open-source AI models. * The initiative addresses the growing demand for AI computing capacity. [IBM](/tag/ibm) and startup [Together AI](/tag/together+ai) have entered a $240 million multi-year agreement to establish a substantial artificial intelligence (AI) cluster on [IBM Cloud](/tag/ibm+cloud), leveraging [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia)'s advanced systems, the companies announced. This infrastructure expansion is designed to support inference for [open-source AI](/tag/open-source+ai) models, a segment gaining traction as businesses seek to manage AI costs and mitigate cybersecurity concerns associated with proprietary models. [AI inference](/tag/ai+inference), which involves running trained AI models to generate responses, has emerged as a primary driver for increased computing capacity. This demand has prompted major cloud providers and chipmakers to invest billions in expanding [AI infrastructure](/tag/ai+infrastructure). The new cluster on IBM Cloud will integrate Nvidia’s [HGX B300](/tag/hgx+b300) systems, which link the chipmaker’s newer [Blackwell](/tag/blackwell) processors, along with its Spectrum-X Ethernet networking gear. Nvidia has indicated that its Blackwell chips are specifically optimised for AI inference workloads. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

The chipmaker's recent announcement of a $20 billion stock offering—upsized from an initial $15 billion—signals management's confidence in capitalizing on unprecedented demand for AI computing hardware. This capital raise represents Intel's first public share sale since its 1971 IPO, underscoring the transformative nature of this moment for the 57-year-old company. The market's enthusiastic response to Intel's AI pivot reflects a fundamental reassessment of the company's strategic position. While Nvidia has dominated headlines with its GPU supremacy, Intel is carving out a critical niche in purpose-built AI silicon, advanced packaging, and foundry services that address the industry's most pressing bottlenecks. The company's focus on "physical AI"—chips designed specifically for AI inference and training workloads—positions it to capture significant value as enterprises rush to deploy AI infrastructure at scale. For investors evaluating Intel's prospects, the key question is whether this rally represents a sustainable re-rating based on fundamentals or a speculative bubble driven by AI fever. Our analysis suggests the transformation is real, but execution risks remain substantial as Intel attempts to simultaneously scale its foundry business, develop competitive AI accelerators, and maintain its traditional CPU dominance in a market increasingly shaped by AI workloads. ## The AI Infrastructure Boom Driving Intel's Revival The artificial intelligence revolution has created an insatiable appetite for specialized computing hardware that extends far beyond the GPU-centric narratives that have dominated investor attention. Data center operators, cloud providers, and enterprises are discovering that AI workloads require diverse silicon architectures optimized for specific tasks—from training massive language models to running inference at the edge. This diversification plays directly to Intel's strengths as the industry's most experienced semiconductor manufacturer with deep expertise in CPU design, memory technologies, and advanced packaging. Intel's stock performance in 2026 reflects this expanding opportunity set. The company's shares have outperformed the broader semiconductor index as investors recognize that the AI buildout will require multiple winners across different chip categories. While Nvidia's GPUs excel at training, Intel's CPUs remain essential for AI inference in data centers, where power efficiency and cost-effectiveness matter as much as raw compute power. The company's Gaudi AI accelerators, though early in their development, represent a credible alternative to Nvidia's dominance in the training market. Major cloud providers are spending tens of billions annually on AI-capable data centers, creating a multi-year demand tailwind for semiconductor suppliers. Key Points [Troogue.ai](https://techobserver.in/topic/troogue-ai/?amp "Posts tagged with Troogue.ai"), a Bengaluru-based technology capability platform, has appointed [Madhusudhana Rao Podila](https://techobserver.in/topic/madhusudhana-rao-podila/?amp "Posts tagged with Madhusudhana Rao Podila") as chief product and technology officer, the company announced on Tuesday (11 August). Podila joins from Thoughtworks, where he served as a senior leader in the data and artificial intelligence domain. The [appointment](https://techobserver.in/topic/appointment/?amp "Posts tagged with Appointment") comes as Troogue plans to expand beyond its existing capability marketplace into building AI agents and what the company calls a Human Intelligence Data Layer. AI agents are software programmes that can perform tasks autonomously on behalf of users, while the Human Intelligence Data Layer is designed to aggregate verified skills, assessment data and work outcomes to create profiles of technology professionals. Troogue’s current marketplace allows enterprises to find, assess and hire technology professionals and teams. The company now plans to develop AI tools that would assist both enterprises and individual professionals throughout the hiring and capability assessment process. ## **Podila’s mandate** In his new role, Podila will be responsible for product vision, technology strategy and engineering execution. He will work with the founding team as Troogue scales its enterprise platform and expands its product offerings. “What attracted me to Troogue is the opportunity to solve a much larger problem than talent matching,” Podila said. “The marketplace gives [us](https://techobserver.in/topic/us/?amp "Posts tagged with US") a strong foundation; the next opportunity is to build intelligent products and AI agents that help enterprises make better capability decisions, while enabling professionals to demonstrate and grow their value.” Madhu Rajputra Peravalli, co-founder and CEO, Troogue, said the company needed expertise in data, AI and large-scale enterprise technology for its next phase. “Enterprises no longer need more access to resumes; they need greater confidence in capability,” Peravalli said. “As Troogue evolves from a capability marketplace into a broader AI-led platform, Madhusudhan brings the depth in data, AI, enterprise technology and large-scale transformation that we need for this next phase.” ## **Podila’s c****areer background** Podila is an alumnus of the Indian Institute of Management Calcutta and has over two decades of experience in the technology sector. Before Thoughtworks, he held roles at Infosys and Four Soft. His experience spans enterprise technology strategy, data and AI platforms, architecture and product-led transformation. Highlighting the event is the world premiere of MiTAC's latest OCP-compliant HPC servers—the C2810Z6 and C2610Z6—developed in collaboration with AMD to harness the all-new 6th Gen AMD EPYC™ Server CPUs on the advanced SP7/SP8 platforms with PCIe Gen 6 connectivity. To meet the demands of continuous Multi-Agent Reasoning Loops and extreme data throughput, MiTAC has engineered comprehensive rack-scale solutions centered around its flagship 52U high-density AI liquid-cooled rack. By incorporating integrated AI servers that span AMD and Intel platforms alongside the NVIDIA accelerated computing platform—featuring compute, networking, and software—MiTAC provides a seamless upgrade path from underlying silicon to a ready-to-deploy 'AI Factory'. **Premiering Next-Gen OCP Compute Nodes for Agentic Execution** As autonomous agents transition from simple prompts to dynamic multi-step workflows, foundational compute nodes require unprecedented I/O bandwidth and power efficiency. At OCP APAC, MiTAC is debuting two ORv3 compute platforms powered by 6th Gen AMD EPYC™ Server CPUs. Featuring AMD's "Zen 6" architecture, PCIe Gen 6 connectivity, and CXL 3.1 support, these platforms are engineered to process massive parallel agent requests while optimizing data center footprint and energy density. MiTAC leads this architectural transition with two world-premiere platforms: **Diversified Rack-Scale Infrastructure for Agentic Workloads** Beyond raw node performance, powering autonomous Agentic AI introduces complex architectural demands. Unlike static single-prompt AI, multi-agent systems rely on continuous reasoning loops, dynamic tool calling, real-time memory retrieval, and multi-agent orchestration. To eliminate thermal, storage, and cluster governance bottlenecks across these execution pipelines, MiTAC Computing delivers a complete spectrum of diversified rack-scale infrastructure: **From Chips to Applications: MiTAC's Full-Stack AI Factory Vision** To bring these diversified components together into an operational environment, MiTAC aligns its entire rack-scale portfolio across ecosystem layers to transform modular silicon into deployment-ready enterprise AI factories: **About MiTAC Computing Technology Corporation** MiTAC Computing Technology Corp., a subsidiary of MiTAC Holdings, delivers comprehensive, energy-efficient server solutions backed by industry expertise dating back to the 1990s. Specializing in AI, HPC, cloud, and edge computing, MiTAC Computing employs rigorous methodologies to ensure uncompromising quality—across barebones, systems, racks, and cluster levels—fully achieving performance and integration. This commitment to quality at every level sets MiTAC Computing apart in the industry. With a worldwide presence and end-to-end capabilities—from R&D and manufacturing to global support—MiTAC Computing provides agile, customized platforms for hyperscale data centers, HPC, and AI applications, ensuring optimal performance and scalability to meet unique business needs. By leveraging the latest advancements in AI and liquid cooling, and unifying the MiTAC brand with Intel DSG and TYAN server products, MiTAC Computing stands out for its innovative, efficient, and reliable server technology as well as its hardware and software integrated solutions—empowering businesses to meet future challenges. The latest development cycle added more than 1,100 lines of code and connected previously separate components into a working pipeline. Rewards are paid in MON, Monad's native token.* CoinFello, the first AI agentic product for using and automating all of DeFi from a single interface launched their latest agent, Fello 2, today. This major upgrade to Fello unlocks the ability for users to describe any onchain strategy in plain language. This means Fello will first understand the user's intent, build out a plan for their review, and upon the user's approval, keep it running in the background so that they can get on with their day. Doing DeFi manually usually means cross-referencing countless values across countless dApps, initiating and approving each transaction, and hoping that the order details are all correctly configured. Fello 2 replaces that with a single prompt. A user can write a complicated prompt for a DeFi strategy, such as, "*Every Friday, move some idle USDC into the best stablecoin pool, but if any position gets within 15% of liquidation, add margin first, then tell me what you did*," and the agent reads each condition, carries out the steps in order, and reports back at the point the user asked to hear about. CoinFello describes the shift simply: instead of doing DeFi, you describe it. For EOA users, getting started requires nothing. Ask Fello to monitor your positions and it will flag anything that matters (a drift, a liquidation risk, a better yield elsewhere), without funding a new wallet. It's only when users want Fello to act on those alerts, and move funds, that they are asked to fund an Automation Wallet they own. Fello 2 also reviews and intelligently judges what it is asked to sign. It declines blind-signing requests, approval-phishing attempts, and transactions built to drain a wallet, and it will not take broader permissions than a user grants. The agent also never holds a user's keys. It works through a delegation model that gives it only the permissions the user grants, and any permission can be revoked at any time. ****A rewards program where you earn from your own swaps and swaps from the people you refer**** The launch coincides with a new Rewards Program. Every eligible swap a user makes through Fello earns them a share of the swap fees, paid in MON. Users also earn a share of the fees generated by anyone they refer, for as long as that person keeps swapping. During a limited launch period, CoinFello will return all of the swap fees it generates on eligible activity to users and their referrers. When that period ends, users and referrers are expected to keep earning at the program's standard rate. The company said it will publish details of the standard split and the timing of the change before the launch period ends. Rewards from both sources are itemized on a Rewards dashboard in the CoinFello app and can be claimed to a wallet the user controls. There is no stated cap on the number of referrals a user can make or the amount that can be earned through qualifying activity. CoinFello also plans to let users deposit claimed rewards into a self-custodial account managed by Fello with the goal of compounding the earnings; that feature is under development and not yet available. *The hardest part of DeFi isn't one thing, it's two: knowing the right move, and then actually making it, over and over again. LLMs.titleZh: Argonne-Led CoLA Approach Makes LLM Pre-Training More Efficient
LLMs.content: ### TCI Media: Home of the Wire Publications ![Header Logo 1](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/ai-600-300x73-1.webp) ![Header Logo 2](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/bigdatawire-logo.webp) ![Header Logo 3](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/qc-600-300x69-1.webp) ![Logo](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/hpc-logo-300x60-1.jpg) ## Off the Wire Press Releases ### August 12, 2026 ### August 11, 2026 ### August 10, 2026 ### August 7, 2026 ## Argonne-Led CoLA Approach Makes LLM Pre-Training More Efficient Aug. 12, 2026 — CoLA might sound like a soft drink, but in computing it’s a new approach for pre-training large language models (LLMs). Developed by researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy’s [Argonne National Laboratory](https://www.anl.gov/), the University of California, Santa Barbara and the University at Albany, SUNY, Compute-Efficient Pre-Training of LLMs via Low-Rank Activation (CoLA) aims to make model training faster, cheaper and more efficient. ![](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/cola_web_1-300x169.jpg) By reducing the number of activation functions, CoLA-M greatly improves the memory saving, outperforming even the “vanilla” implementation of gradient checkpointing (GCP). **Breaking Free from an Unsustainable Trend** LLMs keep becoming bigger, needing more GPUs to provide the necessary power for pre-training over longer periods of time. Researchers have tried to address this trend by simplifying models using ​“low-rank” techniques, but many of these approaches increase computing costs, use too much memory or reduce model quality. CoLA takes a different path. Instead of relying on very large and complex layers commonly used in LLMs, CoLA uses *bottleneck-structured auto-encoders,* comprising low-weight matrices and a nonlinear activation in the middle. Normally, the word *bottleneck* sounds like a bad thing — a place where everything slows down. In CoLA, however, the bottleneck structure is intentional and helpful. “The key insight is that many of the model activations in pre-trained LLMs are redundant,” said Ziyue Liu, a PhD candidate at UC Santa Barbara and a visiting student at Argonne’s Mathematics and Computer Science (MCS) division. ​“By selecting the rank to be significantly smaller than the input/output dimensions, we create a narrow ​‘bottleneck’ that forces the data into a smaller space. Working in this space, CoLA avoids carrying out inefficient, redundant operations and focuses only on what matters most.” When tested with popular LLaMA models, CoLA used fewer parameters and cut computations by about half — without hurting performance during training. **Providing a New Variant** Just as cola soft drinks come in different flavors, CoLA provides a variant, CoLA-M, specifically designed to save memory. “Again, we take advantage of the bottleneck structure,” said Ruijie Zhang, a predoctoral appointee in Argonne’s MCS division and a co-author of the CoLA study. ​“Our CoLA-M implementation stores only the low-rank activations and recomputes the rest when needed, instead of keeping everything in memory. This approach significantly reduces memory demands without slowing down training.” Compared with other memory-saving techniques — which often add extra computation or reduce accuracy — CoLA-M performs exceptionally well. It cuts overall memory use by about two-thirds, surpassing even the most effective implementation (i.e., ​“vanilla” gradient checkpointing, GCP, which saves only one intermediate result from each transformer layer) while being 5x cheaper in precomputation and 3x cheaper in total computation. **Faster Training, Too** Efficiency isn’t just about computation and memory — it’s also about speed. Many existing low-rank methods slow training because they add extra steps. In contrast, both CoLA and CoLA-M deliver higher training throughput...

### Report: Cloud Crime on the Rise as Attackers Exploit Trust ### Key Takeaways Cyber attackers are increasingly turning the technologies and relationships organizations trust most — including cloud identities, AI tools, software dependencies and legitimate authentication processes — into paths for intrusion, according to CrowdStrike's latest threat-hunting research. The [CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/resources/reports/threat-hunting-report/), based on activity observed from July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026, documents a 171% increase in cloud-conscious eCrime activity as financially motivated adversaries pursued credentials, cryptomining capacity, large language model access, and digital financial assets. ![](https://pubads.g.doubleclick.net/gampad/ad?iu=/5978/eof.cam/news&t=item%253d9e49aac8_ba07_40ea_b64a_90f07d33d0ca%26pos%253dbox_c1%26Topic%253dResearch%252cSecurity_and_Safety%252cArtificial_Intelligence%252cBreaking_News%252cResearch_Reports%252cCentral_IT%252cIT_Leadership%252cSecurity_Executives%252cARTICLE_TYPE%252cAUDIENCE&sz=300x250|640x481&tile=4&c=123456789) The cloud finding is part of a broader shift running through the 59-page report. Rather than simply breaking through an external perimeter and moving laterally across endpoints, adversaries are increasingly entering through trusted accounts, tokens, applications and software components. Once authenticated, they can operate inside cloud and software-as-a-service (SaaS) environments using mechanisms that resemble legitimate business activity. LLMs.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) ![](https://img.youtube.com/vi/iqloyWCGYQQ/hqdefault.jpg) [Beyond Static Intelligence: Evaluating Continual Learning — Parth Asawa, UC Berkeley](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iqloyWCGYQQ) GuestParth Asawa 7 hours ago00:20:15en ![](/images/img_default_profile@2x.png)[AI Engineer](/podcast?source=AI%20Engineer) ## Key Takeaways UC Berkeley researcher Parth Asawa argues that current language model benchmarks fail to measure continual learning and proposes a new benchmark with six task domains and gain metrics, showing that vanilla in-context learning outperforms more complex context management systems, and emphasizes that continual learning should be a first-order design consideration. ## Summary Parth Asawa, a PhD student at UC Berkeley, opens his twenty-minute talk with a complaint aimed squarely at his own field: AI researchers gather at conferences to marvel at how capable their agents are, but almost nobody measures whether those agents actually learn. Asawa’s central case, recorded for a conference audience and published August 12, 2026, is that the prevailing evaluation paradigm for language models is built on a strange fiction — that every task begins with a wiped memory. A model is asked to solve one benchmark, then an unrelated one, then another; the scores are aggregated into leaderboards; and the model’s prior experience is never allowed to influence the next attempt. That, he argues, measures point capability, not learning. Against that backdrop, Asawa introduces Continual Learning Bench (CL Bench 1.0), a benchmark built with collaborators at Berkeley, Snorkel AI, the University of Washington, and the University of Wisconsin–Madison. It spans six task domains — from signal processing to poker to sales forecasting — each designed so that prior experience can plausibly improve later performance, and each scored not just on raw reward but on a “gain” metric that isolates learning from base model strength. The headline result is counterintuitive: vanilla in-context learning — simply dumping prior experience into the prompt with no memory management — beat every more elaborate context management system, both on cumulative reward and on reward-versus-cost Pareto frontiers. Asawa interprets the benchmark’s failure modes through the stability-plasticity trade-off, then closes with a broader argument: continual learning should be designed from first principles as a single training phase, not retrofitted onto frozen checkpoints — a position he ties to a research agenda questioning how AI research itself is funded, consolidated, and evaluated. ## The amnesia premise of mainstream model evaluation Asawa’s starting observation is about the shape of the charts that accompany every new model release: one task, then a completely independent task, then another, repeated across benchmarks and aggregated into leaderboards. The implicit assumption, he says, is that the model forgets everything between attempts. > “Imagine if your life was like that. You're restarting from scratch every single time you do anything. That's the premise under which we're evaluating language models today.” Against that, he offers a working definition of continual learning: *sample-efficient online learning that is stable over long horizons.* That definition carries a dual demand — retaining prior information without catastrophic forgetting, while updating priors from new data as it arrives. FastFlowLM is a technology company delivering software designed to handle large language models and AI workloads. (Credit: iStock/BlackJack3D) KINGSTON, R.I. – Aug 12, 2026 – A guiding principle of the University of Rhode Island’s College of Engineering is tracing a line directly from academia to real-world application. Last month that connection was made even stronger. FastFlowLM, founded by URI professor of computer engineering Ken Qing Yang and his former University of Rhode Island colleagues Tao Wei, a professor of engineering at Clemson University who remains on the URI faculty as an adjunct professor, and Alfred Xu, assistant research professor at Clemson and former research assistant at URI, have recently joined California-based semiconductor company AMD. ![](https://www.uri.edu/news/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2026/08/Yangpreferred.jpg-683x1024.jpg) FastFlowLM, was founded by URI professor of computer engineering Ken Qing Yang and his former colleagues Tao Wei, a professor of engineering at Clemson University who remains on the URI faculty as an adjunct professor, and Alfred Xu. (Credit: URI) [FastFlowLM](https://fastflowlm.com/) is a technology company delivering software designed to handle large language models and AI workloads. The FastFlowLM team joining AMD is significant given AMD’s influence in the technology sector. AMD plays a central role across the computing landscape, providing the CPUs, GPUs and AI accelerators that power everything from consumer PCs and gaming platforms to large-scale AI and cloud infrastructure. Many newer computers include a dedicated neural processing unit, or NPU, designed to handle AI workloads. FastFlowLM’s software makes more efficient use of those chips, [allowing workloads to use 2 orders of magnitude larger context](https://fastflowlm.com/benchmarks/)—the units of information used by large language models—more quickly while consuming less power. The result is faster performance, reduced energy consumption, and the ability to run long context AI applications locally without sending data to the cloud. Today’s agentic workloads have grown beyond simple Chat, and are now typically long sessions with growing memory, and context. This requires a highly efficient technology that can support these large session context sizes without sacrificing performance. “AI comes in two parts, model training and inferences. When you use ChatGPT, the response you get is inference. We developed a highly optimized inference software that runs on an NPU,” said Yang. “A state-of-art software can probably handle 2,000 tokens on an NPU. We developed FastFlowLM to speed up that AI inference—with the ability to handle up to half a million tokens.” The idea for FastFlowLM emerged from research conducted by Yang, Wei, and Xu while the three were at URI. Last month that connection was made even stronger. FastFlowLM, founded by URI professor of computer engineering Ken Qing Yang and his former University of Rhode Island colleagues Tao Wei, a professor of engineering at Clemson University who remains on the URI faculty as an adjunct professor, and Alfred Xu, assistant research professor at Clemson and former research assistant at URI, have recently joined California-based semiconductor company AMD. ![](https://www.uri.edu/news/wp-content/uploads/news/sites/16/2026/08/Yangpreferred.jpg-683x1024.jpg) FastFlowLM, was founded by URI professor of computer engineering Ken Qing Yang and his former colleagues Tao Wei, a professor of engineering at Clemson University who remains on the URI faculty as an adjunct professor, and Alfred Xu. (Credit: URI) [FastFlowLM](https://fastflowlm.com/) is a technology company delivering software designed to handle large language models and AI workloads. The FastFlowLM team joining AMD is significant given AMD’s influence in the technology sector. AMD plays a central role across the computing landscape, providing the CPUs, GPUs and AI accelerators that power everything from consumer PCs and gaming platforms to large-scale AI and cloud infrastructure. Many newer computers include a dedicated neural processing unit, or NPU, designed to handle AI workloads. FastFlowLM’s software makes more efficient use of those chips, [allowing workloads to use 2 orders of magnitude larger context](https://fastflowlm.com/benchmarks/)—the units of information used by large language models—more quickly while consuming less power. The result is faster performance, reduced energy consumption, and the ability to run long context AI applications locally without sending data to the cloud. Today’s agentic workloads have grown beyond simple Chat, and are now typically long sessions with growing memory, and context. This requires a highly efficient technology that can support these large session context sizes without sacrificing performance. “AI comes in two parts, model training and inferences. When you use ChatGPT, the response you get is inference. We developed a highly optimized inference software that runs on an NPU,” said Yang. “A state-of-art software can probably handle 2,000 tokens on an NPU. AI Product.content: # Cognition AI Eyes $40B+ Valuation in New Funding Talks: Report ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-10.png) [**Peter Thiel**](https://www.linkedin.com/in/peterthiel/)-backed artificial intelligence startup [**Cognition AI**](https://cognition.com/) is reportedly in early discussions with investors about a new funding round that could value the company at **$40 billion or more**, underscoring the intense investor appetite for companies building AI-powered software development tools. The potential valuation would represent an increase of more than 50% from Cognition’s most recent financing. Less than three months ago, the company raised approximately **$1 billion at a $26 billion valuation**, according to a Bloomberg News report. The new discussions come as Cognition’s business is expanding rapidly. The company’s **annualized revenue run rate is approaching $1 billion**, roughly twice the level reported around the time of its previous financing, Bloomberg said. Cognition has emerged as one of the most closely watched startups in the increasingly competitive market for AI coding tools. Its flagship product, **Devin**, is an autonomous software engineering agent designed to perform development tasks that traditionally require human programmers, including writing and debugging code and completing broader engineering projects. Enterprise adoption of Devin has helped fuel Cognition’s growth. Customers include **Goldman Sachs**, **Mercedes-Benz** and several U.S. government agencies, giving the startup a foothold among large organizations looking to incorporate generative AI into software development workflows. A $40 billion financing would also highlight the extraordinary pace at which valuations for leading AI startups have climbed as investors compete for exposure to companies demonstrating substantial revenue growth. Cognition has attracted backing from prominent technology investors, including billionaire entrepreneur and venture capitalist **Peter Thiel**. The company was founded in 2023 and gained widespread attention after unveiling Devin in 2024 as what it described as an AI software engineer capable of independently handling complex coding assignments. The reported fundraising talks remain at an early stage, and the ultimate size, participants, and valuation of any financing could change. Still, the discussions illustrate how AI coding has become one of the technology sector’s most closely watched markets. Developers and enterprises are increasingly adopting AI systems that can generate code, troubleshoot software and automate portions of the engineering process, creating a potentially large market for companies able to turn those capabilities into enterprise products. AI Product.content: [Skip to content](#content) [![](https://theaiinsider.tech/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/AI-INSIDER_mono.svg)](https://theaiinsider.tech) * [AI](https://theaiinsider.tech/category/ai/), [AI Funding & Investment](https://theaiinsider.tech/category/business/ai-funding-investment/), [Exclusives](https://theaiinsider.tech/category/exclusives/) # AI Competitive Intelligence: How to Track Rival Moves * [James Dargan](https://theaiinsider.tech/author/jamesdargan/) * 7 min read ![](https://theaiinsider.tech/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-07-07-at-08.29.19-1.png) A competitor no longer needs a press release to change the ground under a business. A model upgrade, a quiet price cut, or a single well-placed mention in a ChatGPT answer can shift customer decisions before anyone on the other side even notices. That speed is why competitive intelligence has become one of the more consequential disciplines in AI-era business strategy, and why the tools and methods used to track rivals in 2026 look meaningfully different from the spreadsheet-and-Google-Alert approach of just a few years ago. Understanding what to track, how to evaluate it, and how to turn signal into action is now a core competency rather than a side project. ### WHAT COUNTS AS A SIGNAL WORTH TRACKING The Institute of AI Product Management frames the discipline around four categories that matter most for AI-driven businesses: model capability releases, competitor product launches, pricing and packaging changes, and customer win and loss data. Every major foundation model release resets the capability baseline available to competitors, and the practical question is not whether to respond but how quickly, and what the shift means for competitive advantage. Pricing moves deserve particular scrutiny, since a price cut enabled by genuine cost efficiency behaves very differently from one that simply absorbs margin or swaps in a cheaper underlying model, and that distinction determines how durable the cut is likely to be. Win and loss interviews remain, in the Institute’s framing, the highest-signal data available, since a customer who evaluated a rival and chose them can explain exactly what mattered in that decision. Tiger Tail expands the list of trackable signals to include job postings, website micro-changes, content velocity, ad creative rotation, and review sentiment, arguing that AI tools can now catch patterns human analysts routinely miss. A cluster of machine learning engineer job postings, for instance, often signals a strategic bet weeks or months before any public announcement, and one competitive intelligence firm cited in Tiger Tail’s research found that job posting analysis predicted roughly 67% of major product pivots at least 90 days ahead of time. Website changes that never get announced, a new pricing page layout or an added use case on a features page, similarly reflect quiet shifts in positioning that a manual weekly check is unlikely to catch consistently. ### THE NEWEST BATTLEGROUND: AI SEARCH RESULTS Perhaps the most significant shift in 2026 is that competitive visibility no longer lives only on a search results page. Cognizo’s research describes how AI answer engines, ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, and similar tools, synthesize a response and name a short list of brands rather than presenting ten ranked links for a buyer to scan. Being absent from that shortlist, Cognizo argues, is more damaging than ranking on page two of Google ever was, because the buyer often never sees an alternative. Citing Gartner, the firm notes that traditional search engine volume is projected to drop 25% by 2026 as buyers shift queries to AI chatbots, while separate research from Seer Interactive found that organic click-through rates for informational queries featuring Google AI Overviews fell 61% since mid-2024. shared credential pool is the tradeoff By [Jackie Manning](https://www.techtimes.com/reporters/jackie-manning) [Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324176/20260812/grok-bot-launches-any-app-no-api-all-bots-share-one-cloud-computer-every-login.htm) [Share on Twitter](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=Grok+Bot+Launches%3A+Any+App%2C+No+API%2C+But+All+Bots+Share+One+Cloud+Computer+and+Every+Login+https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324176/20260812/grok-bot-launches-any-app-no-api-all-bots-share-one-cloud-computer-every-login.htm) [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.techtimes.com%2Farticles%2F324176%2F20260812%2Fgrok-bot-launches-any-app-no-api-all-bots-share-one-cloud-computer-every-login.htm&title=Grok+Bot+Launches%3A+Any+App%2C+No+API%2C+But+All+Bots+Share+One+Cloud+Computer+and+Every+Login) [Share on Reddit](http://reddit.com/submit?url=https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324176/20260812/grok-bot-launches-any-app-no-api-all-bots-share-one-cloud-computer-every-login.htm&title=Grok+Bot+Launches%3A+Any+App%2C+No+API%2C+But+All+Bots+Share+One+Cloud+Computer+and+Every+Login) [Share on Flipboard](https://flipboard.com) [Share on Pocket](https://getpocket.com/edit?url=https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324176/20260812/grok-bot-launches-any-app-no-api-all-bots-share-one-cloud-computer-every-login.htm) X.ai SpaceXAI opened early beta access to Grok Bot on August 11, 2026, introducing a category of AI tool that its own documentation describes in terms you should read carefully before handing it your passwords: every bot you create shares one cloud computer, one set of browser sessions, and one credential pool — and the [docs explicitly warn](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/computer-and-apps) you not to treat separate bots as a security boundary. That design choice is also what makes the product compelling. Open Source AI.content: # Nvidia Releases Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Its First Open-Source AI Model under Jensen Huang’s New Push Nvidia launches Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, its first open-source AI model, as CEO Jensen Huang pushes open AI for cybersecurity, sovereignty, and chip sales. By [**Samarjit Kaur**](https://www.convergence-now.com/author/samarjitk/) on August 12, 2026 ##### Share ![Nvidia Releases Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Its First Open-Source AI Model under Jensen Huang’s New Push](https://www.convergence-now.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Nvidia-unveils-first-open-source.jpg.jpeg) Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang unveils the company's push into open-source AI with the release of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning Nvidia has launched Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. It’s a new open-source AI model. The company calls it “lightweight.” It can run on a single GPU on a laptop or desktop. This is Nvidia’s first open-source model since CEO Jensen Huang publicly backed open AI last month. Companies can download, use, and modify it for free. No permission or payment is needed. ## Why Nvidia Is Betting on Open Source Huang made his stance clear in July. He posted on X for the first time to defend open-weight models. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” he wrote. The move followed growing debate in Washington. China’s Moonshot AI had released a model called Kimi K3. It closed the gap with top U.S. models. Lawmakers raised concerns about national security and possible IP theft through a method called distillation. **Also Read**: [AI Agents Set to Replace App-First Smartphones as Tech Industry Shifts Towards Intent-Driven Mobile Experiences](https://www.convergence-now.com/artificial-intelligence/ai-agents-set-to-replace-app-first-smartphones-as-tech-industry-shifts-towards-intent-driven-mobile-experiences/) Huang responded with an open letter. He argued open models help companies stay in control, boost competition, and lower costs. Days later, Nvidia launched an AI safety consortium with Microsoft and other partners. For Nvidia, open-source AI also makes business sense. These models still need GPUs to run. Cheaper AI could mean more chip sales, especially against paid rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic. As Huang put it, “Free AI should be great for hardware. Free AI should be great for chips.” ## Built for AI Agents Nvidia says Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is designed for AI agents. These are programs that can run tasks on their own in the background. Companies like CrowdStrike, CodeRabbit, and Harvey have already tested it. The model is available on HuggingFace and Nvidia’s website. Nvidia also released new software called NeMo Switchyard. It picks the most cost-effective AI model for a given task. **Also Read**: [Samsung to Bring India-Specific AI Features to Next Galaxy Smartphones](https://www.convergence-now.com/artificial-intelligence/samsung-to-bring-india-specific-ai-features-to-next-galaxy-smartphones/) Nvidia says it used distillation to give Nemotron 3.5 Lightning capabilities similar to its larger models. The release adds to a bigger industry shift. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg also pushed open-source AI this week, releasing a coding model called Muse Spark. ![Samarjit Kaur](https://convergence-now.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/1705326483267.jpg) [Samarjit Kaur](https://www.convergence-now.com/author/samarjitk/) Samarjit Kaur is a journalist and communications professional covering technology & emerging digital trends. Open Source AI.content: [Home](/en) Article # Jensen Huang has launched an open-source AI model, which is open to developers for free. 36氪的朋友们2026-08-12 11:21 What kind of computing power layout is hidden behind Jensen Huang's strong promotion of open-source AI? Less than three weeks after Jensen Huang announced his public support for open-source models, NVIDIA has taken practical action. On August 11 local time in the United States, NVIDIA released the open-source model Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, and launched the open-source model routing library NeMo Switchyard at the same time. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is a 30-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model designed for long-running agents, which is mainly responsible for high-frequency tasks such as code review, tool invocation, security alert monitoring, and billing Q&A. NeMo Switchyard is responsible for model selection, routing between different models according to the requirements of tasks. Enterprises can download, use and modify this Nemotron model for free, without obtaining NVIDIA's permission or paying any fees. NVIDIA said that the output speed of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning can reach up to 4 times that of similar models, and the task completion speed of agents is increased by 30%. Internal tests of NeMo Switchyard show that **while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy, the task cost can be reduced to nearly one-third of that of using Opus 4.8 alone**. ## **01 Specially built for high-frequency tasks of Agents** The AI competition in the past few years centered on model scale, but now the era of agents puts more emphasis on the efficiency of models in performing specific tasks. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is the model launched by NVIDIA for this demand. In a complex agent system, more powerful reasoning models can be responsible for task planning, while Nemotron 3.5 Lightning handles a large number of repetitive, execution-oriented tasks. This can reduce the number of large model invocations and lower operating costs at the same time. NVIDIA verified this direction in its self-developed agent task evaluation benchmark PinchBench test. Tests show that Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is about 30% faster in completing tasks while matching the accuracy of Qwen 3.6-35B; under similar completion time, its accuracy is higher than that of Gemma 4-26B. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is the fastest among similar models with state-of-the-art accuracy However, in terms of general capabilities, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is not the highest-level model at present. According to the Intelligence Index of third-party evaluation agency Artificial Analysis, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning covers 9 evaluations with a score of 24, which is on a par with gpt-oss-120b and lower than some larger models. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is customized exclusively for high-frequency agent tasks NVIDIA puts more emphasis on the efficiency and availability of this model in real workloads. At present, many companies have begun to test the application of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning in specific businesses. CrowdStrike has used Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for cybersecurity, Harvey and Trajectory for legal services, CodeRabbit and Baseten for code review, LilaSciences for physics and life science tasks, and FastinoLabs for customizing software development, finance and healthcare workloads. The enterprise-customized Nemotron 3.5 Lightning has extremely high accuracy in professional agent tasks Enterprises can also continue to adjust the model based on their own data. Open Source AI.content: ### TCI Media: Home of the Wire Publications ![Header Logo 1](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/ai-600-300x73-1.webp) ![Header Logo 2](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/bigdatawire-logo.webp) ![Header Logo 3](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/qc-600-300x69-1.webp) ![Logo](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/hpc-logo-300x60-1.jpg) ## Off the Wire Press Releases ### August 12, 2026 ### August 11, 2026 ### August 10, 2026 ### August 7, 2026 ## Argonne-Led CoLA Approach Makes LLM Pre-Training More Efficient Aug. 12, 2026 — CoLA might sound like a soft drink, but in computing it’s a new approach for pre-training large language models (LLMs). Developed by researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy’s [Argonne National Laboratory](https://www.anl.gov/), the University of California, Santa Barbara and the University at Albany, SUNY, Compute-Efficient Pre-Training of LLMs via Low-Rank Activation (CoLA) aims to make model training faster, cheaper and more efficient. ![](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/cola_web_1-300x169.jpg) By reducing the number of activation functions, CoLA-M greatly improves the memory saving, outperforming even the “vanilla” implementation of gradient checkpointing (GCP). **Breaking Free from an Unsustainable Trend** LLMs keep becoming bigger, needing more GPUs to provide the necessary power for pre-training over longer periods of time. Researchers have tried to address this trend by simplifying models using ​“low-rank” techniques, but many of these approaches increase computing costs, use too much memory or reduce model quality. CoLA takes a different path. Instead of relying on very large and complex layers commonly used in LLMs, CoLA uses *bottleneck-structured auto-encoders,* comprising low-weight matrices and a nonlinear activation in the middle. Normally, the word *bottleneck* sounds like a bad thing — a place where everything slows down. In CoLA, however, the bottleneck structure is intentional and helpful. “The key insight is that many of the model activations in pre-trained LLMs are redundant,” said Ziyue Liu, a PhD candidate at UC Santa Barbara and a visiting student at Argonne’s Mathematics and Computer Science (MCS) division. ​“By selecting the rank to be significantly smaller than the input/output dimensions, we create a narrow ​‘bottleneck’ that forces the data into a smaller space. Working in this space, CoLA avoids carrying out inefficient, redundant operations and focuses only on what matters most.” When tested with popular LLaMA models, CoLA used fewer parameters and cut computations by about half — without hurting performance during training. **Providing a New Variant** Just as cola soft drinks come in different flavors, CoLA provides a variant, CoLA-M, specifically designed to save memory. “Again, we take advantage of the bottleneck structure,” said Ruijie Zhang, a predoctoral appointee in Argonne’s MCS division and a co-author of the CoLA study. ​“Our CoLA-M implementation stores only the low-rank activations and recomputes the rest when needed, instead of keeping everything in memory. This approach significantly reduces memory demands without slowing down training.” Compared with other memory-saving techniques — which often add extra computation or reduce accuracy — CoLA-M performs exceptionally well. It cuts overall memory use by about two-thirds, surpassing even the most effective implementation (i.e., ​“vanilla” gradient checkpointing, GCP, which saves only one intermediate result from each transformer layer) while being 5x cheaper in precomputation and 3x cheaper in total computation. **Faster Training, Too** Efficiency isn’t just about computation and memory — it’s also about speed. Many existing low-rank methods slow training because they add extra steps. In contrast, both CoLA and CoLA-M deliver higher training throughput...

The new family of models, dubbed Nemotron 4, is aimed at competing with top open-source models around the world. The flagship model in this series is expected to have at least one trillion parameters. Development progress ### Model's training still being finalized While NVIDIA has not officially announced a release date for Nemotron 4, employees working on the project believe it could be ready by late fall. The company is still finalizing the model's training. This development comes as NVIDIA continues to prioritize AI safety and open AI technologies, having recently partnered with other companies to create tools for improving these areas. Industry impact ### NVIDIA's push for open-source AI NVIDIA is one of the few major US companies to release open-source models. The move has gained traction this year as AI costs rise and affordable Chinese models get closer to the performance of top systems from leading American labs such as [Anthropic](https://www.newsbytesapp.com/news/business/anthropic) and [OpenAI](https://www.newsbytesapp.com/news/business/openai). Last month, NVIDIA signed an open letter with tech giants like Microsoft, supporting open-weight models for broader innovation access. ADVERTISEMENT New releases ### Recent advancements in Nemotron series Separately, NVIDIA recently launched the Nemotron 3.5 Lightning model. The new addition is aimed at tasks such as code review, tool use, security alert monitoring, and answering billing questions. The company also launched NeMo Switchyard, an open-source model-routing library that automatically determines the best-suited AI models for specific tasks. ADVERTISEMENT

[Signup](/reader/signup) ![ad_close_btn](/static/images/svg%20icons/cross_svg.svg) Powered by : # IBM and Together AI sign multi-year deal to scale open-source AI inference with NVIDIA AI Infrastructure on IBM Cloud ## First large-scale inference cluster with Together AI on IBM Cloud using NVIDIA HGX B300 systems to help enterprises run AI workloads, designed for fast and efficient production ![author-image](https://img-cdn.publive.online/fit-in/100x0/filters:format(webp)/dq/media/member_avatars/2026/05/05/2026-05-05t075600035z-500x500-dq-2026-05-05-13-25-58.png ) ![](/static/images/google_news.png) Follow Us ![](/static/images/google_news.png) ![IBM](https://img-cdn.publive.online/fit-in/1280x960/filters:format(webp)/dq/media/media_files/2026/08/12/ibm-2026-08-12-18-48-02.jpg) IBM has announced a collaboration with Together AI to deliver IBM and NVIDIA AI infrastructure. Under a multi-year $240M agreement between IBM and Together AI, IBM is positioned to deploy a large cluster of NVIDIA HGX B300 systems on IBM Cloud with expected availability in Q1 2027. Together AI will use this cluster to provide open-source model inference. This deployment is the first dedicated, large-scale cluster built for inference on IBM Cloud using HGX B300 systems and NVIDIA Spectrum-XTM Ethernet networking. According to NVIDIA, it is built to deliver 30x more AI factory output compared to prior generations. This collaboration aims to enable Together AI to deliver better performance and token economics to enterprises as they look to efficiently scale their AI deployments. Together AI is built on the principle that open-source models are essential for the future of AI and developers should be able to build using open, modular stacks. The company recently raised an $800M Series C financing round at an $8.3B valuation to expand its AI Native Cloud and its platform spans capabilities across inference, training, fine tuning, and agentic workflows. The company reports that it has seen significant momentum for its inference product, now serving 400 trillion tokens monthly. Together AI selected IBM with NVIDIA because of their innovative product roadmaps and their ability to deliver GPU capacity at the pace required for rapid AI scaling and lowest token cost. Building on IBM's expertise in delivering enterprise-grade cloud capabilities, this collaboration aims to help Together AI will continue its expansion into the enterprise space, while making open-source AI more accessible to developers and enterprises around the world. "Enterprises want the performance of the best frontier models without the closed-model price tag, and that only works if the infrastructure underneath is fast and reliable at scale," said Vipul Ved Prakash, CEO at Together AI. "Working alongside IBM with NVIDIA gives us that foundation. Cerebras' super-fast inference solution should help it gain a foothold in the huge market. AMD is aggressively tackling inference from multiple angles. Inference has become the fastest-growing part of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure market, and Bloomberg Intelligence projects it will double the size of the AI training market by 2032, reaching $1.3 trillion. With so much at stake, both leading chipmakers and upstarts are jockeying to grab a slice of this huge, fast-growing market. **Nvidia**(NASDAQ: NVDA), **Cerebras**(NASDAQ: CBRS), and **Advanced Micro Devices**(NASDAQ: AMD) are all tackling this market in different ways. The company's big move to capture share was its "acquisition" of Groq and its language processing units (LPUs). Inference is more about fast memory access and low latency than raw compute power, and LPUs help address this by having SRAM (static random-access memory) embedded directly on their chips. LPUs are particularly useful during the decode phase of inference, which is when large language models (LLMs) answer queries. As such, Nvidia now offers complete systems designed specifically for inference, where its graphics processing units (GPUs) handle the pre-fill phase (reading the prompt) while its LPUs handle the decode phase, thereby speeding up response times. This is a nice solution and positions Nvidia to remain an AI infrastructure leader, even if it doesn't capture the same market share it does in training. ## 2. [IBM](/tag/ibm) and startup [Together AI](/tag/together+ai) have entered a $240 million multi-year agreement to establish a substantial artificial intelligence (AI) cluster on [IBM Cloud](/tag/ibm+cloud), leveraging [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia)'s advanced systems, the companies announced. The chipmaker's recent announcement of a $20 billion stock offering—upsized from an initial $15 billion—signals management's confidence in capitalizing on unprecedented demand for AI computing hardware. This capital raise represents Intel's first public share sale since its 1971 IPO, underscoring the transformative nature of this moment for the 57-year-old company. The market's enthusiastic response to Intel's AI pivot reflects a fundamental reassessment of the company's strategic position. While Nvidia has dominated headlines with its GPU supremacy, Intel is carving out a critical niche in purpose-built AI silicon, advanced packaging, and foundry services that address the industry's most pressing bottlenecks. The company's focus on "physical AI"—chips designed specifically for AI inference and training workloads—positions it to capture significant value as enterprises rush to deploy AI infrastructure at scale. For investors evaluating Intel's prospects, the key question is whether this rally represents a sustainable re-rating based on fundamentals or a speculative bubble driven by AI fever. Our analysis suggests the transformation is real, but execution risks remain substantial as Intel attempts to simultaneously scale its foundry business, develop competitive AI accelerators, and maintain its traditional CPU dominance in a market increasingly shaped by AI workloads. ## The AI Infrastructure Boom Driving Intel's Revival The artificial intelligence revolution has created an insatiable appetite for specialized computing hardware that extends far beyond the GPU-centric narratives that have dominated investor attention. Data center operators, cloud providers, and enterprises are discovering that AI workloads require diverse silicon architectures optimized for specific tasks—from training massive language models to running inference at the edge. This diversification plays directly to Intel's strengths as the industry's most experienced semiconductor manufacturer with deep expertise in CPU design, memory technologies, and advanced packaging. Intel's stock performance in 2026 reflects this expanding opportunity set. The company's shares have outperformed the broader semiconductor index as investors recognize that the AI buildout will require multiple winners across different chip categories. While Nvidia's GPUs excel at training, Intel's CPUs remain essential for AI inference in data centers, where power efficiency and cost-effectiveness matter as much as raw compute power. The company's Gaudi AI accelerators, though early in their development, represent a credible alternative to Nvidia's dominance in the training market. The scale of investment flowing into AI infrastructure is staggering. Major cloud providers are spending tens of billions annually on AI-capable data centers, creating a multi-year demand tailwind for semiconductor suppliers. Morgan Stanley analyst Erik Woodring pointed to recent commentary from the big four hyperscalers -- **Amazon**, **Microsoft**, **Alphabet**, and **Meta Platforms** -- with all four companies talking about industry capacity constraints. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia.
